title: Breeding Dwarf Fortress with Minecraft using AI
author: Key_Cauliflower4565
selftext:
I’ve always really liked the idea of games like Dwarf Fortress, it’s complexity that makes game incredibly repayable and ascii aesthetic, but I am terrible at managing an ever growing population lol.

I’ve always wanted something more like that but where I control my own character surviving and building things in an ASCII world.

So I introduce you guys, **Wild Ascii Craft**, a top down survival/crafting sandbox that I am building with AI.

Limited to ascii codes for visual is definitely tough when adding new mobs but so far I didn’t hit the limit yet thankfully.

I am terrible at publicly sharing my process early so I already spent about 3-4 days into this but still there are a lot of UX improvements and game elements to add.

For this first video I am mostly showing the very early game progression:

0. gathering berries, wood and olives from the ground

1. making some basic materials

2. building a workbench

3. crafting tools

4. digging underground

5. mining resources

6. placing torches so the mine starts becoming an actual place



There are already quite a few systems beyond what I’m showing here, but I don’t really want to dump everything into one post. I think it might be more fun to slowly show how the world and crafting systems are growing.

Crafting is big part of the game too. As you craft a tool, each tools will have procedurally generated traits. As you use higher quality materials to craft items you get better traits. 

I’m also figuring out how to structure a bigger AI-assisted project as I go. I’m using ChatGPT and keeping separate files for the current state of the game, design rules and future ideas so new chats don’t completely lose track of everything lol.

I am doing this to avoid using Codex since chats seem to be almost unlimited(in Plus Plan), I have not hit the limit with just using chat to code the game.

I’ve also been looking at older games for ideas. Recently *Elite (1984)* got me thinking about how much of the world really needs to be saved versus regenerated from the seed, which helped me cut down my world saves file size quite a bit. If anyone is interested I can go more into the AI workflow, project structure or stuff like the save system in another post.  
  
Current goal of the game is to survive as long as possible since there are alot of ways that you can die. Your food storage system could attract pests, your armory could attract bandits trying to steal them. Each region will hack some of the resources that will help you progress the game, so trading with another settlement is also important. 

Since a lot of people here are also experimenting with AI game development, I’m curious what you guys would want to see in a game like this.

If you saw this basic gathering → tools → mining loop, what would make you curious enough to keep going deeper?

I am studying other Ascii games like NetHack and Cataclysm so I am looking forward to how this game shapes itself.

  
**TL;DR:** I’m trying build a single-character ASCII survival/crafting sandbox with procedural tools and lots of possibility like Dwarf Fortress. Curious what you guys would want to see me add or explore next.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
The save-vs-regenerate question you raised at the end is the one I'd dig into, because it turned out to be load-bearing for us in a way I didn't expect.



I work on a persistent-world text game — different genre, same problem: the world has to keep existing between sessions and I can't store all of it. The rule we landed on is that anything the player has never interacted with gets regenerated from the seed, and the instant a player touches something it's promoted to authored state and never regenerated again. Cheap, and it keeps saves small.



The part that bit us is the boundary. If promotion isn't explicit and atomic you get objects that exist in one system and not another — a place a player already walked into that the generator later re-creates as a fresh empty copy. Those ghosts are miserable to debug because nothing errors; the world is just quietly wrong. If you go the Elite route I'd make "has this been touched" one authoritative flag the generator reads, rather than inferring it from whether a record happens to exist.



Two other things we got wrong that seem relevant to a survival sim with pests, bandits and regions:



A world that advances unattended will drift, and the driver is player turns, not wall-clock. We advanced the world on a timer and assumed that made it feel alive. It didn't — worlds with no players just accumulated junk state, and the junk scaled with how much simulated activity we ran, not with how long they sat. Tying advancement to actual player action fixed more "this world feels incoherent" complaints than any content work did.



Unbounded emergence is noise. We let consequences propagate through the entity graph — you rob someone, their faction reacts, their rivals react. Great at two hops, incoherent by four, so we hard-capped traversal depth. Same story with spawning: one of our zones went from 15 locations to 64 because the spawn rule never consulted a cap, and it stopped being a place and became a list.



To your actual question — the gather to tools to mining loop wouldn't hold me on its own. What would is the first time the world does something to me that I can trace back to a specific thing I did three sessions ago. Your "food storage attracts pests" idea is exactly that, and I'd push it further than feels reasonable: bandits who remember they got repelled, a region that's measurably poorer because I stripped it. Consequence with an address is the whole game.



Happy to go deeper on the state-promotion boundary if it's useful — it's the part I'd do differently from scratch.
